title: The thread and the king
hook: Lakshmi ties a thread on a king's wrist to bring Vishnu home; why the rakhi prayer names King Bali
carry: a rakhi binds a promise you keep

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pillar of light with no end, and a flower that lied. Your line was the lingam is a sign of the endless light.
screen: `MAHA SHIVARATRI: A SIGN OF THE ENDLESS LIGHT.`

segments.voice: There was once a king named Bali, an asura king, and he never said no to anyone who asked him for anything. That habit cost him his whole kingdom; on day one hundred fifty-four you'll hear how. He ended up ruling a world below this one, and Vishnu, moved by his goodness, promised to stand guard at his door. Which left Vishnu's wife, the goddess Lakshmi, alone at home. So one full moon, many families say, she goes down to Bali's palace in disguise, with a thread in her hand.
screen: `A KING WHO NEVER SAID NO.` → `VISHNU GUARDS HIS DOOR.` → `LAKSHMI, WITH A THREAD.`

segments.voice: She ties the thread on Bali's wrist and calls him brother. A sister! Ask for anything. And Lakshmi asks for the one thing she came for: the guard at your door. Bali, who has never broken his word, lets Vishnu go home. It's a story many families tell for Raksha Bandhan, and though it isn't in the oldest texts, it echoes in the prayer. When the thread is tied, many priests and some families say a short Sanskrit verse that begins yena baddho bali raja. Its sense: with the thread that bound mighty King Bali, I bind you; hold fast, don't slip. Bound how? The old story says Vamana had him tied with Varuna's ropes, but many teachers read the real bond as his word: Bali never broke it. That's the teaching under the rakhi. Raksha means protection, bandhan a bond, and the thread is a promise made before God. In Hindu teaching, keeping your word is part of dharma, the right way to live, and Bali is a model of it: he kept his promises even when they cost him everything. In many homes, the sister circles a small lamp before her brother's face, puts a red tilak on his forehead, ties the thread on his right wrist, and feeds him a sweet. He gives a gift and a promise to protect her. Today rakhis are tied between sisters, cousins and close friends too. And today: a rakhi isn't a bracelet. It's a promise you can see on your wrist all week, and it asks Bali's question: will you keep it when it costs you something?
screen: `LAKSHMI TIES, BALI KEEPS HIS WORD.` · `YENA BADDHO BALI RAJA.` · `RAKSHA, PROTECTION. BANDHAN, A BOND.` · `LAMP, TILAK, THREAD, SWEET, PROMISE.` · then, large: `A PROMISE YOU CAN SEE.`

segments.voice: Think of one promise you've made to someone, out loud or not: to show up, to look out for them, to call. If you have a thread, tie it on your wrist; if not, just rest your fingers where a rakhi would go. If you pray, say the name you pray to. Then make the promise again, silently, once, and hold your wrist for a few breaths. Then let your hand go.
Raksha Bandhan. The bond of protection: a thread tied on the full moon of Shravan, with a promise that holds.
Your line: a rakhi binds a promise you keep. Bound like Bali, by his word. One hundred fifty days now.

Bali.meaning: the generous asura king who never broke his word

Lakshmi.meaning: the goddess of fortune, Vishnu's wife

dharma.meaning: the right way to live; duty

Shravan.meaning: a monsoon month in the Hindu calendar

tilak.meaning: a mark of red powder on the forehead

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 8.22–8.23 (Bali sent to Sutala; Vishnu promises to guard his door)
Bhavishya Purana, Uttara Parva (the raksha rite and the verse 'yena baddho bali raja')
Raksha Bandhan observance; the popular telling of Lakshmi tying a rakhi on Bali

notes: Indrani (Shachi) tying a raksha on Indra: Bhavishya Purana, Uttara Parva 137. Confirm the reference.
Order of the ritual (arti, tilak with akshat, rakhi on right wrist, sweet, gift and promise): common but varies by family. Confirm.

Avani Avittam/upakarma: renewal of the yajnopavita on Shravan Purnima (for Rig and Yajur Vedins), mainly among communities who wear it. Written as 'in many South Indian families, men who wear the sacred thread'. Confirm.
Narali Purnima coconut offering by coastal (Koli) communities in Maharashtra. Confirm.
Tying rakhis on trees (vriksha bandhan): a modern practice. Confirm.
